segments.text: Surah Al-Ikhlas — Reflections
Verses 1–4
Verse 1
Say: “He is Allah, the One[1];
Allah introduces Himself to us in a few words that convey a truth the heart cannot do without:
Say: “He is Allah, the One[1];

In His mercy, He did not provide food for people’s bodies and leave their souls without guidance. He sent messengers, revealed scriptures, and made His revelation a source of life and light, as He says:
Likewise, We have revealed to you a revelation by Our command.
One of the greatest ways this revelation brings the heart to life is by acquainting it with its Lord.

So we should not read Surah Al-Ikhlas as words a Muslim has known since childhood and therefore need not pause over. Its words may remain in our memory while their influence fades from our fears, hopes, and choices.
The opening
Say:
is a command.

The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, conveyed the surah just as it was revealed to him, including the word of command itself. He neither composed his own description of Allah nor left out any of the revelation he received.
The inclusion of this command reminds us that the oneness of Allah is to be learned and taught, rather than kept as private knowledge.

A Muslim receives what Allah has made known about Himself, then teaches it to others with the clarity of the Quran, without letting complicated expressions and arguments become a barrier between people and this truth.
The word rendered
He
has been understood as a pronoun that introduces a matter of great importance: it prepares the listener for something momentous that deserves close attention—Allah’s unique oneness.
“Allah” is the proper name of our Lord, glorified is He. The word Ahad then affirms His uniqueness: He is One in His essence, attributes, and actions, with no partner in any of them.

One proposed distinction between al-Wahid and al-Ahad is that the oneness meant here is more than counting one as opposed to two: it is uniqueness without equal in the perfection of His essence, attributes, and actions.
To keep this from remaining an abstract idea, reflect on what you have read in the Quran about Allah’s actions.
You see who saves from destruction, supports the oppressed, destroys the oppressor, heals the sick, and guides those who have gone astray:
every day He is engaged in some matters[1]
When you reach this surah near the end of the Quran, it is as though it answers a question stirring in your heart: Who has done all of this? It is Allah, the One.
It was Allah who saved Abraham from the fire. When Abraham was thrown into it, he said:
Allah is Sufficient for us, and He is the best Protector[3].
The divine command came:
O fire, be cool and safe for Abraham.
It was Allah who protected Joseph from the women’s schemes. Joseph said,
Unless you protect me from their guile, I may succumb to them
, and his Lord answered his prayer and protected him from their schemes.
It was Allah who heard Jonah in the darkness of the whale’s belly and saved him. Jonah called out,
None has the right to be worshiped except You. Glory be to You! I have certainly done wrong
, and the answer came:
So We answered his prayer and rescued him from distress.
The ordeals differ—a fire, a temptation, distress in the depths of darkness—but the One who has the power to deliver from them is the same.
You encounter this knowledge again when you read of Pharaoh’s drowning, Allah’s kindness to Joseph in prison, or His help for the believers at Badr despite their weakness:
Allah had helped you at Badr when you were weak
. The actions of the one Lord are varied; His servant comes to know Him through these accounts as well as through verses describing His names and attributes.
When your heart longs for His kindness and mercy, you know where to turn. Then come His words:
Allah, the Eternal Refuge[1].
This helps us understand the greatness of the surah despite its brevity. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said that Surah Al-Ikhlas
is equivalent to a third of the Qur'an.

A listener might expect a surah of such standing to be long, yet it has only four verses. This draws attention to the weight of the meaning they bring together, rather than merely the number of their words.

The same lesson is reinforced by what happened when the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, asked Ubayy ibn Ka‘b about the greatest verse in Allah’s Book. Ubayy named Ayat al-Kursi; the Prophet affirmed his answer and congratulated him on his knowledge.
It is a verse that makes Allah known through His knowledge, His sustaining of all things, and His dominion.
Likewise, Al-Fatihah, which the Prophet described as the greatest surah in the Quran, brings together praise of Allah and the plea for His guidance.

In seeking the Quran’s guidance, we should not pass over these clear meanings to pursue subtle insights alone. Reflection also means allowing a familiar truth to return to the heart, alive and influential, after we have grown used to repeating it.
The verses heard by a group of jinn moved them to declare their faith and renounce worshiping partners with Allah:
that guides to the right way, so we have believed in it, and we will never associate anyone with our Lord.
The fruit of listening is more than admiration for the words: it is knowing the One to be worshiped and devoting worship to Him alone.
This worship is Allah’s right over His creation. It is not a marginal concern to be crowded out by everything else until it is forgotten.
The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, explained to Mu‘adh that Allah’s right over His servants is
that they should worship Him (Alone) and should not worship any besides Him.
People may spend a long time considering their rights over one another, then overlook the right of the One who created them all. The verse brings them back to this foundation.
Acknowledging it is not an empty phrase with no consequences. While Bilal, may Allah be pleased with him, was being tortured, he would say,
Ahad, Ahad (One, One)

His tormentors could hurt his body, but he did not grant them the power to change whom he worshiped. These words declared to whom his servitude belonged, which is why they weighed so heavily on those who wanted to turn him away from his faith.
The biography of the Prophet also records that
One, One!
was the Muslims’ rallying cry at Badr.

The truth that steadied a believer under oppression is the same truth he carries in strength. It is not a belief to abandon when suffering becomes severe or some worldly possession makes him feel self-sufficient.

Every day the heart deals with people and practical means, pulled in different directions by fear, hope, and eager desire. It needs this knowledge renewed, rather than heard once and then left behind.
This is why it is prescribed to repeat the declaration
None has the right to be worshipped but Allah, the Alone Who has no partners, to Him belongs Dominion and to Him belong all the Praises, and He has power over all things
one hundred times in a day.
The words are familiar, but repeating them brings the heart back to the One who governs all things when its surroundings almost distract it from Him.

The merit of Al-Ikhlas encourages frequent recitation. In view of its equivalence to a third of the Quran, it is hoped that someone who recites it three times will receive the reward of reciting the Quran.

Its meanings are renewed in prayer as well: in Witr, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, would recite Al-A‘la, then Al-Kafirun, then Al-Ikhlas; in the two voluntary units before the obligatory dawn prayer, he would recite Al-Kafirun and Al-Ikhlas.
Al-Kafirun renounces the worship of anything besides Allah, while Al-Ikhlas affirms His oneness. This is why Al-Kafirun has also been called a surah of sincere devotion.
In the quiet of the night, the believer reviews his day in light of this truth, drawing on the way night prayer helps bring the tongue and heart into harmony:
Indeed, worship at night is more effective[1] and more conducive to proper recitation[2].
Then, before going out among people, he begins his day by renewing it.

One lesson to reflect on in this repetition between the darkness of night and the light of dawn is that Allah’s oneness does not change as circumstances change. Conditions may grow harsh or ease, and believers may be weak or strong, but their Lord remains One and their worship belongs to Him alone. This truth is not altered for a passing advantage; instead, actions and choices are reconsidered in its light.

publisherNotes.text: [1] He is Alone, without a partner, indivisible and distinct from all else. The only true deity, unique in His essence, attributes, and actions.
[1] He is absolute, perfect, complete, self-sufficient; the one eternally and constantly required and sought; all existence depend upon Him; all matters ultimately return to Him.
[1] Such as giving life and causing death, enriching some and impoverishing others, elevating some and debasing others, etc.
[1] It is reported in an authentic Hadīth that Abraham said, while being thrown into the fire, “Allah is sufficient for us and He is the best Protector.”
[2] The darkness of the night, the sea, and the whale's belly.
[1] Or "getting up at night is more difficult...," meaning that it can only be done by sincere believers.
[2] i.e., for reciting, hearing, and understanding of the Qur’an.

[3] This is one of the greatest Dhikr (remembrance) during times of hardship. Ibn ‘Abbās (رضي الله عنهما) reported: “Hasbunā Allāh wa ni‘ma al-Wakīl (Allah suffices us, He is the best of Protectors), was said by Abraham (عليه السلام) when he was thrown in the fire and was said by Muhammad (ﷺ) when it was said: “People have regrouped for you, so fear them”, their belief grew firmer and they said: “Allah suffices us, He is the best of Protectors”.” [Al-Bukhārī: 4563]

contextNotes.text: This is an inference about hoped-for reward, not a substitute for reading the Quran.
